cur.100.algorithm:
y′ = f(x)g(y) denklemini yazınız.
Değişkenleri ayırınız: dy/g(y) = f(x) dx.
İki tarafı integre ediniz ve tek bir sabit ekleyiniz.
Mümkünse y'yi çözünüz; değilse kapalı bağıntıyı olduğu gibi bırakınız.
g(y) = 0 sabit çözümlerini ekleyiniz ve başlangıç koşulunu uygulayınız.
cur.100.answer: Değişkenleri ayırmak dy/y = 4x/(x² + 1) dx verir. İntegral alınırsa ln|y| = 2 ln(x² + 1) + C olur, dolayısıyla y = C(x² + 1)² elde edilir.
cur.100.idea: Ayrılabilir bir denklem, x'e bağlı bir fonksiyon ile y'ye bağlı bir fonksiyonun çarpımına ayrılır. Tüm y terimlerini bir tarafa, tüm x terimlerini diğer tarafa taşımak problemi iki integrale indirger.
cur.100.pitfall: g(y) ile bölmek g(y) = 0 sabit çözümlerini kaybettirir; bunları ayrıca belirtiniz.
cur.100.theory.0: Separation means keeping each variable with its own differential: $\frac{dy}{g(y)}=f(x)\,dx$. Integrating both sides gives a relation between $y$ and $x$ that need not be explicit; that is why the answer is sometimes kept in the implicit form $F(x,y)=C$.
cur.100.theory.1: The subtle point is dividing by $g(y)$. If $g(y_0)=0$, the constant function $y=y_0$ is also a solution and is lost by the division. These equilibrium solutions must be checked separately; sometimes the initial condition sits exactly on one of them.
cur.101.algorithm:
Denklemi M(x,y) dx + N(x,y) dy = 0 biçiminde yazınız.
M_y = N_x koşulunu sınayınız.
Denklem tamsa M'yi x'e göre integre ediniz ve eksik y fonksiyonunu bulmak için F_y ile N'yi karşılaştırınız.
F(x,y) = C olarak alınız.
Denklem tam değilse μ(x) = e^(∫(M_y − N_x)/N dx) veya buna karşılık gelen μ(y) ifadesini deneyiniz.
cur.101.answer: M_y = 1 = N_x olduğundan denklem tamdır. İntegral almak F = x² + xy + y² verir ve çözüm x² + xy + y² = C olur.
cur.101.idea: Tam bir denklem, bir potansiyel fonksiyon F(x,y)'nin diferansiyelidir. Çözüm F(x,y) = C düzey eğrisidir ve tamlık, karışık türev testiyle belirlenir.
cur.101.pitfall: Tamlık testi M_y = N_x'tir, M_x = N_y değildir; kısmi türevleri karıştırmak sık yapılan hatadır.
cur.101.theory.0: If $F$ exists, $dF=F_x\,dx+F_y\,dy$, so $F_x=M$ and $F_y=N$. The equality of mixed partials $F_{xy}=F_{yx}$ gives $M_y=N_x$. Integrating $M$ with respect to $x$ determines $F$ up to an unknown function of $y$, which is found by comparison with $N$.
cur.101.theory.1: If the condition fails, an integrating factor $\mu(x)$ or $\mu(y)$ sometimes makes the equation exact. Such a factor is not guaranteed to exist, but when it depends on a single variable it is found from a simple differential equation.
cur.102.algorithm:
(x,y) yerine (tx,ty) koymanın f'yi değiştirmediğini, yani y′ = f(y/x) olduğunu doğrulayınız.
y = vx ve y′ = v + xv′ yerine koyunuz.
x dv/dx = f(v) − v biçimine sadeleştiriniz.
Değişkenleri ayırıp integre ediniz: ∫dv/(f(v) − v) = ∫dx/x.
v = y/x geri yerine koyunuz ve f(v) − v = 0 denkleminin çözümlerini ekleyiniz.
cur.102.answer: y = vx ile y′ = v + xv′ olur ve denklem xv′ = 1/v biçimine girer. Böylece v² = 2 ln|x| + C ve y² = x²(2 ln|x| + C) elde edilir.
cur.102.idea: Homojen bir birinci mertebeden denklem, x ve y'ye yalnızca y/x oranı üzerinden bağlıdır. y = vx dönüşümü onu v ve x için ayrılabilir bir denkleme çevirir.
cur.102.pitfall: Homojenliği kontrol etmeden y = vx kullanmayınız; kaydırılmış bir denklem bunun yerine afin dönüşüm gerektirir.
cur.102.theory.0: The word "homogeneous" here is not the same as for a linear equation. It means $f(x,y)$ is unchanged by scaling both variables together: $f(tx,ty)=f(x,y)$. Such a function can be written as a function of the ratio $y/x$, and that ratio is the key to the solution.
cur.102.theory.1: With $y=vx$ and the product rule, $y'=v+xv'$. Substituting into $v+xv'=f(v)$ gives $x\frac{dv}{dx}=f(v)-v$, which is separable. After integrating, replace $v$ by $y/x$. Constant solutions satisfying $f(v)-v=0$ must also be checked separately.
cur.103.algorithm:
y′ + P(x)y = Q(x)yⁿ denklemini yazınız.
yⁿ ile bölünüz.
v = y^(1−n) yerine koyunuz; böylece v′ = (1−n)y^(−n)y′ olur.
Elde edilen lineer denklemi v için çözünüz.
Geri yerine koyunuz ve n > 0 iken y = 0 çözümünü ekleyiniz.
cur.103.answer: Denklemi y′ − y = y² olarak yeniden yazınız; burada n = 2 ve v = y⁻¹ olur. O hâlde v′ + v = −1, v = Ce⁻ˣ − 1 ve y = 1/(Ce⁻ˣ − 1) elde edilir.
cur.103.idea: Bir Bernoulli denklemi, sağ taraftaki y kuvveti dışında lineerdir. v = y^(1−n) dönüşümü bu kuvveti ortadan kaldırır ve lineer bir denklem verir.
cur.103.pitfall: n = 0 ve n = 1 durumlarında denklem Bernoulli değil lineerdir; doğrudan çözünüz.
cur.103.theory.0: For $n\neq 0,1$ the equation is nonlinear, but dividing by $y^n$ and setting $v=y^{1-n}$ linearises it. Since $v'=(1-n)y^{-n}y'$, the equation becomes $v'+(1-n)P(x)v=(1-n)Q(x)$, which is solved with an integrating factor.
cur.103.theory.1: The cases $n=0$ and $n=1$ are already linear and must not be transformed; $n=0$ is an ordinary linear nonhomogeneous equation and $n=1$ is separable. After solving for $v$, return with $y=v^{1/(1-n)}$ and fix the sign of the root from the initial condition.
cur.104.algorithm:
ay″ + by′ + cy = 0 denklemini yazınız.
ar² + br + c = 0 denklemini çözünüz.
Farklı gerçek kökler r₁, r₂ için y = C₁e^{r₁x} + C₂e^{r₂x} kullanınız.
C₁ ve C₂'yi bulmak için başlangıç koşullarını uygulayınız.
Denklemde yerine koyarak doğrulayınız.
cur.104.answer: Karakteristik denklem r² − 3r + 2 = 0 olduğundan r = 1, 2 ve y = C₁eˣ + C₂e²ˣ olur.
cur.104.idea: Sabit katsayılı homojen bir denklem için y = e^{rx} yerine koyunuz. Diferansiyel denklem, ar² + br + c = 0 karakteristik denklemine dönüşür.
cur.104.pitfall: Karakteristik denklemde bilinmeyen y değil r'dir; y'yi denkleme geri koymayınız.
cur.104.theory.0: Because the derivative of $e^{rx}$ is $re^{rx}$, substituting $y=e^{rx}$ turns every term into a coefficient times $e^{rx}$, and $e^{rx}$ factors out. Since $e^{rx}\neq 0$, what remains is the algebraic equation $ar^2+br+c=0$, whose roots determine the behaviour of the solution.
cur.104.theory.1: For distinct real roots $r_1\neq r_2$ there are two independent solutions $e^{r_1x}$ and $e^{r_2x}$, and the general solution is $y=C_1e^{r_1x}+C_2e^{r_2x}$. Their Wronskian is nonzero, so they really form a fundamental set. The signs of the roots decide whether the solution grows, decays or stays constant.
cur.105.algorithm:
Karakteristik denklemi çözünüz.
r = α ± iβ ise α = −b/(2a) ve β = √(4ac − b²)/(2a) değerlerini hesaplayınız.
y = e^{αx}(C₁ cos βx + C₂ sin βx) yazınız.
Başlangıç koşullarını uygulayınız.
Yerine koyarak doğrulayınız.
cur.105.answer: r² + 1 = 0 denklemi r = ±i verir; böylece α = 0, β = 1 ve y = C₁ cos x + C₂ sin x olur.
cur.105.idea: Negatif diskriminant, r = α ± iβ karmaşık eşlenik kök çiftini verir. Euler formülü bu çifti, üstel fonksiyon ile trigonometrik fonksiyonların çarpımı olan gerçek çözümlere dönüştürür.
cur.105.pitfall: α sıfırdan farklıyken e^{αx} çarpanını atmayınız; salınım yine bu üstel ifadeyle çarpılır.
cur.105.theory.0: When $r=\alpha+i\beta$ is a root, $e^{(\alpha+i\beta)x}=e^{\alpha x}(\cos\beta x+i\sin\beta x)$ is a complex solution. Since the coefficients are real, the conjugate is also a solution, and a suitable linear combination gives the two real solutions $e^{\alpha x}\cos\beta x$ and $e^{\alpha x}\sin\beta x$.
cur.105.theory.1: The factor $e^{\alpha x}$ is the amplitude envelope. If $\alpha<0$ the oscillation decays, if $\alpha>0$ it grows, and if $\alpha=0$ it is pure oscillation. $\beta$ is the angular frequency and the period is $\frac{2\pi}{\beta}$. This is exactly the damped oscillator met in mechanical applications.
cur.106.algorithm:
Karakteristik denklemi çözünüz.
r kökü katlıysa y = (C₁ + C₂x)e^{rx} kullanınız.
Genel bir lineer denklemde y = v(x)y₁ alınız.
Yerine koyarak v′ için birinci mertebeden bir denklem elde ediniz.
İki kez integre ediniz ve başlangıç koşullarını uygulayınız.
cur.106.answer: r² + 4r + 4 = (r + 2)² olduğundan r = −2 kökü çift katlıdır ve y = (C₁ + C₂x)e⁻²ˣ olur.
cur.106.idea: Katlı bir karakteristik kök yalnızca bir üstel çözüm verir. İkinci bağımsız çözüm, bunun x ile çarpılmasıyla veya daha genel olarak mertebe indirgeme yoluyla elde edilir.
cur.106.pitfall: Katlı bir kök e^{rx} ifadesinin iki kopyasını vermez; ikinci çözüm için x çarpanı gerekir.
cur.106.theory.0: If $r$ is a double root, $y_1=e^{rx}$ is one solution but a second copy of $e^{rx}$ is not independent. For a second-order constant-coefficient equation the second solution is $y_2=xe^{rx}$, and the general solution is $y=(C_1+C_2x)e^{rx}$.
cur.106.theory.1: The reason is reduction of order: setting $y=u(x)e^{rx}$ and substituting removes the $u$ term and leaves an equation for $u'$ whose solution is $u=C_1+C_2x$. A repeated root usually marks the boundary between non-oscillatory decay and oscillation, as in the critically damped spring.
cur.107.algorithm:
Homojen denklemi çözüp y_h çözümünü bulunuz.
y_p için g(x) ve tüm türevlerinin biçiminde bir deneme yapınız.
Deneme homojen bir çözümle çakışıyorsa onu x ile çarpınız.
y_p ifadesini yerine koyunuz ve benzer terimlerin katsayılarını eşitleyiniz.
y = y_h + y_p alınız ve başlangıç koşullarını uygulayınız.
cur.107.answer: Homojen çözüm C₁eˣ + C₂e²ˣ'dir. eˣ zaten homojen denklemin çözümü olduğundan öneri y_p = Axeˣ biçimindedir. Yerine koymak A = −1 verir, dolayısıyla y = C₁eˣ + C₂e²ˣ − xeˣ.
cur.107.idea: Belirsiz katsayılar yöntemi, zorlayıcı terimle aynı biçimde bir özel çözüm arar, ardından katsayılarını yerine koyarak belirler.
cur.107.pitfall: Zorlayıcı terim homojen bir çözümle çakışıyorsa basit deneme başarısız olur; katsayıları eşitlemeden önce x ile çarpınız.
cur.107.theory.0: If the right side is a polynomial, an exponential, a sine or cosine, or a product of these, the particular solution has the same shape. For example $g(x)=e^{x}$ suggests $y_p=Ae^{x}$, and $g(x)=\cos 2x$ suggests $y_p=A\cos 2x+B\sin 2x$. Substituting and equating coefficients determines $A$ and $B$.
cur.107.theory.1: If the guessed term is itself a solution of the homogeneous equation, the plain guess fails because the left side becomes zero. Then multiply the guess by $x^s$, where $s$ is the multiplicity of that root in the characteristic equation. For a composite $g$, superposition lets you build a particular solution for each piece and add them.
cur.108.algorithm:
Homojen denklemin iki bağımsız çözümü y₁, y₂'yi bulunuz.
y = u₁y₁ + u₂y₂ alınız.
u₁′y₁ + u₂′y₂ = 0 ve u₁′y₁′ + u₂′y₂′ = g denklemlerini çözünüz.
İntegre ederek u₁ ve u₂'yi elde ediniz.
Homojen çözümü ekleyiniz ve başlangıç koşullarını uygulayınız.
cur.108.answer: y₁ = cos x ve y₂ = sin x ile sistem u₁′ = −sin x sec x ve u₂′ = cos x sec x verir. Böylece y = C₁ cos x + C₂ sin x + cos x ln|cos x| + x sin x olur.
cur.108.example: y″ + y = sec x denklemini çözünüz.
cur.108.idea: Sabitlerin değişimi, homojen çözümdeki sabitleri fonksiyonlarla değiştirir. Belirsiz katsayıların aksine, her sürekli zorlayıcı terim için işe yarar.
cur.108.pitfall: Önce denklemi y″ teriminin katsayısına bölünüz; sabitlerin değişimi formülü bu katsayının 1 olmasını varsayar.
cur.108.theory.0: Setting $y=u_1y_1+u_2y_2$ and imposing $u_1'y_1+u_2'y_2=0$ simplifies the derivatives and gives the system $\begin{cases}u_1'y_1+u_2'y_2=0\\ u_1'y_1'+u_2'y_2'=g\end{cases}$. Solving it with the Wronskian $W=y_1y_2'-y_1'y_2$ gives $u_1'=-\frac{y_2g}{W}$ and $u_2'=\frac{y_1g}{W}$.
cur.108.theory.1: After integrating, the particular solution is $y_p=u_1y_1+u_2y_2$. This method is the only analytic route for $g$ such as $\sec x$ or $\ln x$, which have no simple guessed shape. The requirements are that the coefficient of $y''$ equals 1 and that the Wronskian is nonzero on the interval.
cur.109.algorithm:
Karakteristik polinomu yazınız.
Tüm kökleri ve katlılıklarını bulunuz.
m katlı gerçek bir r kökü için e^{rx}, xe^{rx}, …, x^{m−1}e^{rx} terimlerini ekleyiniz.
m katlı bir α ± iβ karmaşık kök çifti için k = 0, …, m−1 olmak üzere e^{αx}x^k cos βx ve e^{αx}x^k sin βx terimlerini ekleyiniz.
Terimleri birleştiriniz ve başlangıç koşullarını uygulayınız.
cur.109.answer: Karakteristik polinom (r − 1)³ olduğundan y = (C₁ + C₂x + C₃x²)eˣ olur.
cur.109.idea: Sabit katsayılı yüksek mertebeden homojen bir denklemde karakteristik polinom tüm çözümleri verir. Gerçek kökler üstel fonksiyonlar, karmaşık kökler salınımlar verir; katlılık ise x'in kuvvetlerini ekler.
cur.109.pitfall: m katlı bir kök m bağımsız çözüm gerektirir; tek bir üstel ifadeyle yetinmeyiniz.
cur.109.theory.0: A characteristic polynomial of degree $n$ has exactly $n$ roots counted with multiplicity. Each real root $r$ of multiplicity $m$ gives the solutions $e^{rx}, xe^{rx},\ldots,x^{m-1}e^{rx}$. Each complex pair $\alpha\pm i\beta$ of multiplicity $m$ gives $x^ke^{\alpha x}\cos\beta x$ and $x^ke^{\alpha x}\sin\beta x$ for $k=0..m-1$.
cur.109.theory.1: Together these solutions form a fundamental set, and the general solution is their linear combination. Because the coefficients are constant, the roots can be found by factoring or numerically. The shape of the roots determines the qualitative behaviour: growth, decay or oscillation.
cur.110.algorithm:
Homojen çözümü bulunuz.
y_p için g ve tüm türevlerinin biçiminde bir deneme yapınız.
Deneme homojen çözümle çakışıyorsa x^s ile çarpınız; burada s, zorlayıcı kökün katlılığıdır.
Yerine koyunuz ve katsayıları eşitleyiniz.
y_h ile y_p'yi toplayınız, ardından başlangıç koşullarını uygulayınız.
cur.110.answer: Homojen kökler 0 (çift katlı) ve 1'dir; dolayısıyla y_h = C₁ + C₂x + C₃eˣ olur. y_p = Axeˣ denemesi A = 1 verir, buradan y = C₁ + C₂x + C₃eˣ + xeˣ elde edilir.
cur.110.idea: Belirsiz katsayılar denemesi her mertebeye genişletilebilir. Zorlayıcı terim bir toplam ise her terim için bir özel çözüm bulup bunları toplayınız.
cur.110.pitfall: Çarpan x^s'dir; burada s, zorlayıcı kökün karakteristik polinomdaki katlılığıdır.
cur.110.theory.0: For an $n$th-order equation with forcing $g$, if $g$ is a combination of polynomials, exponentials and trigonometric terms, the particular solution has the same shape. If a piece of $g$ overlaps a characteristic root, the guess for that piece is multiplied by $x^s$, where $s$ is the multiplicity of that root.
cur.110.theory.1: Superposition says that for $g=g_1+g_2$, if $y_{p1}$ solves $g_1$ and $y_{p2}$ solves $g_2$, then $y_{p1}+y_{p2}$ solves $g$. This splits the guess into smaller problems and avoids one large, error-prone guess.
cur.66.algorithm:
En yüksek mertebeden türevi belirleyiniz; mertebe budur.
Tüm y terimlerini sola, zorlayıcı terimi sağa taşıyınız.
Her y teriminin, x'e bağlı bir katsayı ile y'nin veya y'nin bir türevinin çarpımı olduğunu doğrulayınız.
y'nin bir kuvveti, çarpımı veya doğrusal olmayan bir fonksiyonu görünüyorsa denklem lineer değildir.
Yöntem seçmeden önce mertebeyi, lineerliği ve homojenliği belirleyiniz.
cur.66.answer: Birincisi ikinci mertebeden, lineer ve homojen olmayan bir denklemdir. İkincisi birinci mertebeden ve lineer değildir, çünkü y karesiyle yer alır.
cur.66.example: y″ + 3y′ + 2y = eˣ ve y′ = y² denklemlerini sınıflandırınız.
cur.66.idea: Lineer bir denklem, y'yi ve türevlerini yalnızca birinci kuvvetten içerir; katsayıları yalnızca x'e bağlıdır. y·y′ gibi herhangi bir çarpım veya sin y gibi doğrusal olmayan bir fonksiyon denklemi lineer olmaktan çıkarır.
cur.66.pitfall: Mertebe ve derece farklıdır; birinci mertebeden bir denklem yine de lineer olmayabilir ve her çarpan lineer olsa da y·y′ lineer değildir.
cur.66.theory.0: An $n$th-order linear equation can be written $a_n(x)y^{(n)}+\cdots+a_0(x)y=g(x)$. Two facts matter for this family: the general solution carries as many constants as the order, and superposition holds. Superposition says that if $y_1$ and $y_2$ solve the homogeneous equation, so does every linear combination.
cur.66.theory.1: Nonlinearity is not always bad, but the linear methods do not apply. Terms such as $y^2$, $y\,y'$, $\sin y$ or a coefficient depending on $y$ make the equation nonlinear. An equation can be first order and still nonlinear; the two properties are independent.
cur.67.algorithm:
y′ = f(x,y), y(x₀) = y₀ başlangıç değer problemini yazınız.
f'nin (x₀,y₀) çevresindeki bir dikdörtgende sürekli olduğunu doğrulayınız; bu durumda çözüm vardır.
∂f/∂y'nin de aynı bölgede sürekli olduğunu doğrulayınız; bu durumda çözüm tektir.
Çözüm eğrilerinin kesişmesini elemek için tekliği kullanınız.
Koşullar sağlanmıyorsa birden çok çözüm veya tekil çözüm arayınız.
cur.67.answer: Hem f = y² hem de ∂f/∂y = 2y, (0,1) yakınında süreklidir; bu nedenle çözüm tektir. Çözüm, −∞ < x < 1 için y = 1/(1 − x) olur.
cur.67.example: y′ = y², y(0) = 1 probleminin tek bir çözümü var mıdır?
cur.67.idea: Bir başlangıç değer problemi, verilen bir noktadan geçen çözümü ister. f'nin sürekliliği varlığı, y'ye göre Lipschitz koşulu ise tekliği garanti eder.
cur.67.pitfall: f'nin sürekliliği yalnızca varlığı verir; teklik için f'nin y'ye göre değişim hızına ilişkin bir sınır da gerekir.
cur.67.theory.0: The existence and uniqueness theorem says that if $f$ and $\partial f/\partial y$ are continuous on a rectangle around $(x_0,y_0)$, then $y'=f(x,y)$ with $y(x_0)=y_0$ has a unique solution on some interval containing $x_0$. Continuity of $f$ gives existence, and a bounded $\partial f/\partial y$ gives uniqueness.
cur.67.theory.1: The condition is sufficient, not necessary. If the test fails a unique solution may still exist; for example $f=y^{1/3}$ is continuous at $y=0$ but its derivative is unbounded there. For linear problems, continuity of the coefficients on an interval is enough for existence and uniqueness.
cur.68.algorithm:
y_{n+1} = f(n, y_n) yazınız ve y₀ değerini kaydediniz.
Örüntüyü görmek için ilk birkaç terimi hesaplayınız.
y_{n+1} = a y_n + b için y* = b/(1 − a) sabit noktasını bulunuz.
y_n = y* + (y₀ − y*)aⁿ yazınız.
Kararlılığı kontrol ediniz: |a| < 1 ise yakınsar, |a| > 1 ise ıraksar.
cur.68.answer: Sabit nokta y* = 6 olduğundan y_n = 6 − 5(0.5)ⁿ olur. |0.5| < 1 olduğu için dizi 6'ya yakınsar.
cur.68.idea: Birinci mertebeden bir fark denklemi, çözümü bir tam adımdan sonrakine taşır. Lineer denklemlerin bir sabit noktası ve çarpanın kuvvetleri cinsinden açık bir formülü vardır.
cur.68.pitfall: n indeksi ayrıktır; ona göre türev almayınız veya integral almayınız.
cur.68.theory.0: The fixed point $y^*$ is where the sequence stops changing: $y^*=ay^*+b$, so $y^*=\frac{b}{1-a}$ for $a\neq 1$. Writing $y_n=y^*+(y_0-y^*)\,a^n$ shows that the distance from the fixed point is multiplied by $a$ at each step.
cur.68.theory.1: If $|a|<1$ then $a^n\to 0$ and the sequence converges to $y^*$ (stable). If $|a|>1$ it diverges, and if $a=-1$ it oscillates between two values. The index $n$ is discrete; differentiation and integration with respect to it make no sense, and the tools are summation and iteration.
cur.69.algorithm:
Denklemi F₀ cos ωt zorlayıcı terimiyle standart biçimde yazınız.
Homojen (geçici) çözümü bulunuz.
ω frekansında bir özel çözüm arayınız.
Genliğini ve fazını bulunuz.
İki kısmı toplayınız ve ω doğal frekansa eşit olduğunda rezonansı belirleyiniz.
cur.69.answer: Homojen kısım C₁ cos ω₀t + C₂ sin ω₀t biçimindedir. Özel çözüm F₀ cos ωt/(ω₀² − ω²) olduğundan sistemin yanıtı bu iki kısmın toplamıdır.
cur.69.example: y″ + ω₀²y = F₀ cos ωt denklemini ω ≠ ω₀ için çözünüz.
cur.69.idea: Sinüzoidal zorlamalı bir yay-kütle sistemi, geçici bir homojen kısma ve zorlama frekansında kararlı hâl yanıtına sahiptir. Rezonans, iki frekans çakıştığında ortaya çıkar.
cur.69.pitfall: Rezonansta payda sıfırlanır; bu durumda özel çözüm t sin ω₀t içerir ve sınırsız büyür.
cur.69.theory.0: The equation $my''+cy'+ky=F_0\cos\omega t$ has two parts. The homogeneous solution decays when there is damping and disappears after a while; the particular solution oscillates at the frequency $\omega$ and persists. The steady-state amplitude is proportional to $1/\sqrt{(k-m\omega^2)^2+(c\omega)^2}$.
cur.69.theory.1: The natural frequency is $\omega_0=\sqrt{k/m}$. As $\omega$ approaches $\omega_0$ the denominator shrinks and the amplitude grows. With no damping and $\omega=\omega_0$, the particular solution takes the form $t\sin\omega_0t$ and the amplitude grows without bound; this is resonance. With damping the amplitude becomes large but stays finite.
cur.70.algorithm:
Denklemi y⁽ⁿ⁾ üzerindeki katsayı 1 olacak biçimde yazınız.
Katsayıların ve g'nin aralıkta sürekli olduğunu doğrulayınız.
n bağımsız homojen çözüm bulunuz.
Zorlayıcı terime karşılık gelen bir özel çözüm ekleyiniz.
Tüm sabitleri belirlemek için n başlangıç koşulunu uygulayınız.
cur.70.answer: r³ − 1 = (r − 1)(r² + r + 1) olduğundan kökler 1 ve −1/2 ± i√3/2'dir. Genel çözüm, eˣ ile e^{−x/2} cos(√3x/2) ve e^{−x/2} sin(√3x/2) terimlerini birleştirir.
cur.70.idea: n. mertebeden lineer bir denklemin çözüm uzayı n boyutludur. Katsayıların bir aralıkta sürekli olması, n başlangıç koşulu için çözümün tekliğini garanti eder.
cur.70.pitfall: n. mertebeden bir denklem n bağımsız çözüm ve n başlangıç koşulu gerektirir; her mertebe için bir sabit vardır.
cur.70.theory.0: For $y^{(n)}+p_{n-1}(x)y^{(n-1)}+\cdots+p_0(x)y=g(x)$, if the coefficients and $g$ are continuous on an interval $I$, the initial value problem with $n$ conditions at one point has a unique solution on $I$. A set of $n$ independent solutions is called a fundamental set, and its Wronskian is nonzero on $I$.
cur.70.theory.1: The general solution is the linear combination $y=C_1y_1+\cdots+C_ny_n$ plus one particular solution. For constant coefficients, the characteristic polynomial of degree $n$ determines everything, and each root contributes as many solutions as its multiplicity.
cur.71.algorithm:
Homojen denklemin n bağımsız çözümü y₁, …, y_n'yi bulunuz.
Wronskiyen W'yi hesaplayınız.
Σu_k′y_k = 0, …, Σu_k′y_k^{(n−2)} = 0, Σu_k′y_k^{(n−1)} = g sistemini çözünüz.
İntegre ederek u₁, …, u_n'yi elde ediniz.
y = y_h + Σu_k y_k alınız ve başlangıç koşullarını uygulayınız.
cur.71.answer: Homojen çözümler 1, eˣ ve e⁻ˣ biçimindedir. Sabitlerin değişimi −x özel çözümünü verir; dolayısıyla y = C₁ + C₂eˣ + C₃e⁻ˣ − x olur.
cur.71.idea: Yüksek mertebeden sabitlerin değişimi, n bilinmeyen fonksiyonun türevlerini bulmak için Wronskiyen'i kullanır. Özel çözümü kurmak için bunları integre ediniz.
cur.71.pitfall: Wronskiyen aralıkta sıfırdan farklı olmalıdır; aksi hâlde seçilen çözümler bağımlıdır ve sistemin tek bir çözümü yoktur.
cur.71.theory.0: For an $n$th-order equation, write the particular solution as $y_p=\sum_{i=1}^{n}u_i(x)y_i(x)$ and impose $n-1$ extra conditions so the derivatives simplify. The resulting system is $\sum_i u_i'y_i^{(k)}=0$ for $k=0..n-2$ and $\sum_i u_i'y_i^{(n-1)}=g$.
cur.71.theory.1: Solving this system with the Wronskian $W$ gives $u_i'=\frac{W_i}{W}$, where $W_i$ is the determinant with column $i$ replaced by the right-hand side. After integrating, the particular solution is obtained. The Wronskian must be nonzero on the interval so that the $y_i$ are independent.
cur.98.algorithm:
Denklemi y′ = f(x, y) biçiminde yazınız.
x ve y değerlerinden oluşan bir ızgara seçiniz ve her noktada f'yi hesaplayınız.
Her ızgara noktasına eğimi f olan kısa bir doğru parçası çiziniz.
Parçaları izleyen çözüm eğrilerini çiziniz ve f = 0 olan noktaları işaretleyiniz.
Uzun vadeli davranışı alandan okuyunuz; sayısal bir çözücü bunu doğrular.
cur.98.answer: Eğim y = 0 ve y = 2 üzerinde sıfırdır. Bu doğrular arasındaki çözümler y = 2'ye doğru artar, y = 2'nin üstündeki çözümler ise ona doğru azalır; bu nedenle y = 2 kararlıdır.
cur.98.example: y′ = y(2 − y) denkleminin yön alanını çiziniz.
cur.98.idea: Yön alanı, y′ = f(x,y) eğimini bir noktalar ızgarasında çizer. Çözüm eğrileri bu parçalara teğettir; böylece alan, herhangi bir formül bulunmadan önce büyümeyi, azalmayı ve dengeyi gösterir.
cur.98.pitfall: Yön alanı davranış hakkında fikir verir ancak bir kanıt değildir; çizilen pencere dışındaki tekil çözümleri veya işaret değişimini gözden kaçırabilir.
cur.98.theory.0: A direction field turns a differential equation into a picture. Each segment shows only a slope, not a value, so solutions are read from the field rather than computed from it. Curves that are tangent to the segments at every point are called integral curves.
cur.98.theory.1: If $f$ and $\partial f/\partial y$ are continuous, two integral curves can never cross; two solutions passing through one point would violate uniqueness. The lines where $f=0$ are equilibrium solutions and usually separate the directions of motion.
cur.99.algorithm:
Denklemi y′ + P(x)y = Q(x) standart biçiminde yazınız.
μ = e^(∫P(x) dx) değerini hesaplayınız.
Her terimi μ ile çarpınız.
Sol tarafı (μy)′ olarak yeniden yazınız ve iki tarafı integre ediniz.
y'yi çözünüz, ardından verilmişse başlangıç koşulunu uygulayınız.
cur.99.answer: Burada P = 1/x olduğundan μ = x olur. O hâlde (xy)′ = x³ ve xy = x⁴/4 + C, buradan y = x³/4 + C/x elde edilir.
cur.99.example: y′ + y/x = x² denklemini x > 0 için çözünüz.
cur.99.idea: Birinci mertebeden lineer bir denklem, bir integrasyon çarpanı μ(x) ile çarpılarak tam hâle getirilebilir. Böylece sol taraf μy'nin türevi olur ve tek bir integrasyon çözümü verir.
cur.99.pitfall: P'yi belirlemeden önce denklemi y′ teriminin katsayısına bölünüz; aksi hâlde integrasyon çarpanı yanlış olur.
cur.99.theory.0: The integrating factor comes from the product rule. We want to write $\mu y'+\mu P y$ as $(\mu y)'$. Expanding $(\mu y)'=\mu y'+\mu'y$ shows that $\mu'=\mu P$, that is $\mu=e^{\int P\,dx}$.
cur.99.theory.1: After multiplying, the equation becomes $(\mu y)'=\mu Q$ and only two integrals remain. The interval of validity is the largest interval on which $P$, $Q$ and $\mu$ are continuous and the coefficient of $y'$ does not vanish.

ode.a1: Linear independence is checked on an interval where the functions and W are defined and continuous.
ode.a2: The envelope is defined where F and F_c are smooth and eliminating c is valid.
ode.a3: F is smooth and the family slope is finite where the trajectories are computed; c was eliminated before solving.
ode.c12: RK4 with automatic step subdivision; the plot marks the computed trajectories.
ode.c14: The symbolic W matches the numeric determinant at sampled points.
ode.c17: Envelope is tangent to the family
ode.c18: The implicit slopes of the envelope and of the family agree at the contact point.
ode.c_exact_fail: The symbolic relation was not verified; branch points may exist.
ode.c_exact_ok: $d\mu$ is proportional to $M\,dx + N\,dy$; the solution family is valid.
ode.c_implicit_ok: The implicit relation satisfies y′ = p(y).
ode.c_substitution_fail: Symbolic verification was inconclusive; check the domain.
ode.c_substitution_ok: Differentiating the answer satisfies the equation.
ode.n.autonomous_quadratic: Denklem x ve y'yi açıkça içermiyor. p = y′ ve q = y″ yazıldığında q'ya göre ikinci dereceden bir denklem kalır; her q(p) kökü dx = dp/q ve dy = p·dp/q olarak ayrılır ve (x(p), y(p)) parametrik çözümü elde edilir.
ode.n.clairaut_form: The equation has the Clairaut form $y = xp + f(p)$ with $p = y'$; $f(p) =$ {f}.
ode.n.cofactor_expansion: Cofactor expansion along the first row.
ode.n.differential_form_not_exact: $M\,dx + N\,dy = 0$ is not exact; rewriting it as $y' = -M/N$.
ode.n.eliminate_c_direct: Form the system $F = 0$ and $F_x + F_y\,y' = 0$. Differentiating and simplifying removes $c$, so the derivative equation is already the family ODE.
ode.n.eliminate_c_value: Form the system $F = 0$ and $F_x + F_y\,y' = 0$. From $F = 0$, $c =$ {c}; substituting this into the derivative equation removes $c$ and gives the family ODE.
ode.n.family_parameter_c: F(x,y,c) = 0, where c is the parameter.
ode.n.forcing_ansatz: The forcing term splits into $e^{kx}$, polynomial and sine/cosine pieces. Because $k + ib$ has multiplicity {mult} as a characteristic root, the ansatz is {ansatz}.
ode.n.horizontal_family: The family slope is $0$, so the family is horizontal and the trajectory family is the vertical lines $x = C$.
ode.n.infinite_trajectory_slope: The trajectory slope is infinite, so the family consists of the vertical lines $x = C$.
ode.n.jump_discontinuity: Jump discontinuity: the one-sided limits exist but are different.
ode.n.lagrange_form: The equation has the Lagrange form $y = x\,g(p) + f(p)$ with $p = y'$; $g(p) =$ {g} and $f(p) =$ {f}.
ode.n.lagrange_x_form: Denklem $p = y'$ cinsinden x için çözülmüştür: $x = g(p)$, $g(p) =$ {f}. Türev alınınca $dy/dp = p\,g'(p)$ elde edilir.
ode.n.linear_homogeneous_order: The linear homogeneous equation has constant coefficients of order {n}.
ode.n.no_envelope: This family has no envelope: $\partial F/\partial c = 0$ gives only a family member (or a degenerate curve).
ode.n.not_continuous: The limit does not exist, so the function is not continuous here.
ode.n.numeric_first_order: Desteklenen kapalı form bulunamadı. Aşağıdaki eğriler $y' =$ {rhs} için RK4 yörüngeleridir ve yalnızca sonlu kaldıkları aralıkta geçerlidir.

ode.n11: Verified by substitution into the equation.
ode.n12: With $y = y_1 + 1/z$ and one known particular solution, the nonlinear equation becomes the linear equation $z' + (2P\,y_1 + Q)z = -P$.
ode.n13: With $y = -u'/(Pu)$, the equation becomes $u'' - (Q + P'/P)u' + PR\,u = 0$.
ode.n14: The solution u is obtained, then y = −u′/(P u) returns the Riccati solution.
ode.n15: This is the Bernoulli form $y' + P(x)y = Q(x)y^n$ with $n =$ {n0}, $P =$ {n1} and $Q =$ {n2}.
ode.n16: With $v = y^{1-n}$ the equation becomes linear: $v' +$ {n0} $v =$ {n1}.
ode.n17: The linear equation is solved with an integrating factor to obtain v(x).
ode.n18: Because 1−n is even, solving explicitly for y would drop one branch; the complete family is kept in implicit form.
ode.n19: The substitution $y = v^{1/(1-n)}$ returns to the original variable.
ode.n2: Differentiating both sides and using $y' = p$ gives $(x + f'(p))\,dp/dx = 0$.
ode.n20: After rearrangement: $y' + P(x)y = Q(x)$ with $P =$ {n0} and $Q =$ {n1}.
ode.n21: $\mu = e^{\int P\,dx}$; multiplying by $\mu$ turns both sides into $(\mu y)' = \mu Q$.
ode.n22: Integrating gives $\int \mu Q\,dx =$ {n0}; dividing by $\mu$ isolates $y$ and leaves $C$ free.
ode.n23: Replacing y by v·x leaves an expression that depends on v alone, so the equation is homogeneous: it depends only on the ratio y/x.
ode.n24: With $y = vx$ the product rule gives $y' = v + x\,v'$, so the equation becomes $x\,v' = F(v) - v$.
ode.n25: Here $F(v) = v$, giving the line family $y = Cx$.
ode.n26: The transformed equation is separable: $dv/(F(v) - v) = dx/x$.
ode.n27: Both sides are integrated and share a single constant.
ode.n28: Substituting $v = y/x$ returns to the original variable and gives the implicit solution.
ode.n29: The right side factors as f(x) = {n0} and g(y) = {n1}, so the equation is separable.
ode.n3: The first factor $dp/dx = 0$ gives $p = C$, hence the line family $y = Cx + f(C)$.
ode.n30: Dividing by $g(y)$ gives $dy/g(y) = f(x)\,dx$; each side now has one variable only.
ode.n31: Integrating each side with respect to its own variable, with one shared constant C, gives the implicit solution.
ode.n32: The right side is built from the linear combination ax + by alone, so a single substitution turns it separable.
ode.n33: With $u = ax + y$ we get $u' = a + y'$, so the equation becomes $u' = a + f(u)$, which is separable.
ode.n34: Both sides are integrated, keeping a single shared constant.
ode.n35: Restoring $u = ax + y$ gives the solution of the original equation.
ode.n36: $\partial M/\partial y =$ {n0} and $\partial N/\partial x =$ {n1}; they agree, so the equation is exact and a potential $u$ exists with $\partial u/\partial x = M$ and $\partial u/\partial y = N$.
ode.n37: Integrate $M$ with respect to $x$ (the constant is $\varphi(y)$); comparing $\partial u/\partial y$ with $N$ gives $\varphi'(y) =$ {n0} and $\varphi(y) =$ {n1}.
ode.n38: The level curves of the potential are the solutions, so u(x,y) = C.
ode.n39: $\partial M/\partial y =$ {n0} and $\partial N/\partial x =$ {n1}; they differ, so the original equation is not exact and needs an integrating factor.

ode.n42: The solution family is the level curves of this potential: u(x,y) = C.
ode.n44: A linear combination of the basis functions with arbitrary constants.
ode.n45: Only the order-{n0} derivative and a function of x occur, so the equation can be integrated {n1} times directly.
ode.n46: Integrating lowers the order by one and introduces the constant {n0}.
ode.n47: No term contains y itself, only x and derivatives of y up to order {n0}. This is an equation missing the dependent variable.
ode.n48: Set {n0} $= y'$. Then $y'' =$ {n1}$'$, $y''' =$ {n2}$''$, and in general $y^{(k)} =$ {n3}$^{(k-1)}$; the order drops by one and the equation is written in {n4} and $x$.
ode.n49: In the following steps {n0} is the dependent variable and x is the independent variable; wherever the generic text says y, it means {n1} here.

ode.n50: {n0} could not be isolated explicitly; the same relation is written with {n1} = y′ restored.

ode.n55: {n0} could not be isolated explicitly; the relation is written with {n1} = y′ restored.

study.calculus_series.key_idea.0: A series is a limit of partial sums; grouping or rearranging terms is only safe when the series converges absolutely.
study.calculus_series.key_idea.1: The ratio test settles absolute convergence when $\lim|a_{n+1}/a_n|<1$ and divergence when the limit exceeds $1$.
study.calculus_series.key_idea.2: Taylor's formula writes $f(x)$ as a polynomial plus a remainder $R_n$ that measures the error of the approximation.
study.calculus_series.key_idea.3: The Lagrange remainder $R_n=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(c)}{(n+1)!}(x-a)^{n+1}$ gives a practical error bound.
study.calculus_series.key_idea.4: The radius of convergence is the distance from the centre to the nearest singularity, and the endpoints need separate checking.
study.calculus_series.pitfalls: Do not conclude convergence from the first few terms or from the terms tending to zero. The ratio test is inconclusive at $L=1$; use a comparison or an integral test there. When bounding a Taylor remainder, bound the derivative on the whole interval, not just at the centre.
study.calculus_series.short_answer: A series converges when its partial sums approach a finite limit. Test convergence with the ratio or root test, then use Taylor's formula with a remainder to approximate a function and bound the error.
study.calculus_series.subtitle: Convergence tests, Taylor series, the remainder and the radius of convergence.
study.calculus_series.theory.0: A sequence is a list $a_1,a_2,\ldots$ and a series is the sum of its terms. The series converges when the sequence of partial sums $S_n=a_1+\cdots+a_n$ has a finite limit. The first necessary condition is simple: the terms must tend to zero. It is necessary, not sufficient, as the harmonic series shows.
study.calculus_series.theory.1: The ratio test compares a series with a geometric one. If $\lim\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right|=L<1$ the series converges absolutely; if $L>1$ it diverges; if $L=1$ the test is silent. The root test uses $\lim\sqrt[n]{|a_n|}$ and behaves the same way. Absolute convergence is stronger than convergence and permits rearrangement.
study.calculus_series.theory.2: Taylor's formula with centre $a$ is $f(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k!}(x-a)^k+R_n(x)$. The polynomial is the best local approximation of its degree, and the remainder is not an error of the formula but a description of what is left over.
study.calculus_series.theory.3: The Lagrange form of the remainder is $R_n(x)=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(c)}{(n+1)!}(x-a)^{n+1}$ for some $c$ between $a$ and $x$. If you can bound the derivative on that interval, you get a numerical bound on the error, which is exactly what a calculator needs.
study.calculus_series.theory.4: A power series $\sum a_n(x-a)^n$ converges on an interval $(a-R,a+R)$ and may converge at either endpoint. The radius is computed from the ratio test or from the distance to the nearest complex singularity. Inside the interval the series can be differentiated and integrated term by term.
study.calculus_series.theory.5: The standard expansions are worth memorising: $e^x$, $\sin x$, $\cos x$, $\frac{1}{1-x}$ and $\ln(1+x)$. Most others are derived from these by substitution, multiplication or integration, which is faster than computing derivatives from scratch.

study.derivative.key_idea.0: Average rate of change is a secant slope; the derivative is the limit as the two points merge.
study.derivative.key_idea.1: Power, product, quotient and chain rules turn the limit definition into fast algebra.
study.derivative.key_idea.2: A derivative is a function in its own right: f′ can be differentiated again to get f″.
study.derivative.key_idea.3: Implicit differentiation handles curves written as F(x, y) = 0, not just y = f(x).
study.derivative.key_idea.4: The sign of f′ gives increasing/decreasing behaviour; the sign of f″ gives concavity.
study.derivative.pitfalls: The usual mistakes are forgetting the chain rule inside a composite function and treating the derivative as an average slope. A derivative is local: it depends on the behaviour arbitrarily close to the point.
study.derivative.short_answer: The derivative is the instantaneous rate of change of a function. It is the limit of the difference quotient and equals the slope of the tangent line at that point.
study.derivative.subtitle: Instantaneous rate of change, the tangent line and the rules that make differentiation mechanical.
study.derivative.theory.0: A precise definition grows out of a simple idea. To get the slope of a curve at $x_0$, take two nearby points and compute the slope of the secant line. As the gap $h$ shrinks to zero, that slope tends to the tangent slope: $f'(x_0)=\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(x_0+h)-f(x_0)}{h}$. If this limit exists and is finite, the function is differentiable there. Differentiability is stronger than continuity: every differentiable function is continuous, but not conversely (take $|x|$ at zero).
study.derivative.theory.1: We do not have to take a limit every time. A few rules do all the work: the power rule $\frac{d}{dx}x^n=nx^{n-1}$, the product rule $\frac{d}{dx}(fg)=f'g+fg'$, the quotient rule $\frac{d}{dx}\frac{f}{g}=\frac{f'g-fg'}{g^2}$, and above all the chain rule $\frac{d}{dx}f(g(x))=f'(g(x))\,g'(x)$. Any function built from sums, products, quotients and compositions differentiates with these four rules.
study.derivative.theory.2: The derivative is written $f'(x)$, $y'$ or $\frac{dy}{dx}$. Because it is a function, it can be differentiated again: $f''$ or $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$. For motion on a line, if $s(t)$ is position then $s'(t)$ is velocity and $s''(t)$ is acceleration; the same reading returns when second-order differential equations are modelled.
study.derivative.theory.3: Near $x=a$ every differentiable curve looks like its tangent. That observation gives the linear approximation $f(x)\approx f(a)+f'(a)(x-a)$. The error is of order $(x-a)^2$, which is why the approximation is excellent for small changes. This is also the idea behind linearisation and Euler's method for solving differential equations numerically.
study.derivative.theory.4: The sign of the derivative reveals the behaviour: $f'>0$ means increasing, $f'<0$ decreasing, and $f'=0$ marks a critical point. The second derivative shows concavity; $f''>0$ curves upward and $f''<0$ curves downward. The mean value theorem guarantees that on an interval where the function is continuous and differentiable inside, some point has instantaneous slope equal to the average slope across the interval.
study.derivative.theory.5: Sometimes a curve is not given explicitly as $y=f(x)$ but implicitly by $F(x,y)=0$. Then we differentiate both sides with respect to $x$ and solve for $y'$ as the unknown; this is implicit differentiation. For circles and ellipses, where solving for $y$ is awkward, it is the only practical way to get the slope.

study.first_order.key_idea.1: A linear equation $y'+P(x)y=Q(x)$ becomes exact after multiplying by $\mu(x)=e^{\int P\,dx}$.
study.first_order.key_idea.2: An exact equation $M\,dx+N\,dy=0$ has a potential $F$ with $F_x=M$, $F_y=N$, and its solutions are the level curves $F(x,y)=C$.

When you build an integrating factor, read $P$ from the coefficient of $y$ in standard form, not from the original equation.
study.first_order.short_answer: A first-order equation contains $y'$ but no higher derivative. Most textbook problems belong to four families: separable, linear, exact and Bernoulli. Classify first, apply the matching method, and use the initial condition to fix the constant.
study.first_order.subtitle: Separable, linear, exact and Bernoulli equations, and the integrating factor that solves the linear family.
study.first_order.theory.0: A first-order equation relates $x$, $y$ and $y'$ only. Geometrically it assigns a slope to every point of the plane, so its solutions are curves that follow this slope field. The general solution carries one arbitrary constant, and a single initial condition selects one curve from the family.
study.first_order.theory.1: For the linear equation $y'+P(x)y=Q(x)$ multiply by $\mu(x)=e^{\int P(x)\,dx}$. The left side collapses to $(\mu y)'=\mu Q$, so $y=\frac{1}{\mu}\int \mu Q\,dx$. This is the most useful formula of the chapter: every linear problem is one integration away from its answer.
study.first_order.theory.2: A separable equation $y'=f(x)g(y)$ is solved by separating variables, $\frac{dy}{g(y)}=f(x)\,dx$, and integrating. The constant appears on one side. An implicit answer is acceptable until the initial condition lets you solve for $y$ explicitly.
study.first_order.theory.3: An exact equation $M\,dx+N\,dy=0$ satisfies $M_y=N_x$. Then there is a potential $F$ with $F_x=M$ and $F_y=N$, found by integrating $M$ in $x$ and matching the remaining terms. Solutions are the level curves $F(x,y)=C$. When the equation is not exact, an integrating factor that depends on $x$ alone or on $y$ alone often repairs it.
study.first_order.theory.4: Bernoulli equations have the form $y'+P(x)y=Q(x)y^n$ with $n\ne0,1$. The substitution $v=y^{1-n}$ produces the linear equation $v'+(1-n)Pv=(1-n)Q$. The same substitution explains why $n=1$ is already linear and $n=0$ is separable.
study.first_order.theory.5: Existence and uniqueness are local. If $P$ and $Q$ are continuous on an interval containing $x_0$, the linear problem has exactly one solution there. For nonlinear equations the hypothesis is continuity of $f$ and $\partial f/\partial y$. The guarantee holds only inside the rectangle, so the interval can be short: the solution of $y'=y^2$ blows up in finite time.

study.integral.key_idea.0: A Riemann sum approximates area with rectangles; the integral is the limit as the rectangles get thin.
study.integral.key_idea.1: An antiderivative reverses differentiation, so every derivative rule has an integral counterpart.
study.integral.key_idea.2: Substitution reverses the chain rule; integration by parts reverses the product rule.
study.integral.key_idea.3: Area below the axis counts as negative, which is why the integral is called signed area.
study.integral.key_idea.4: Improper integrals take a limit at an infinite endpoint or a singularity.
study.integral.pitfalls: Do not drop the constant of integration in an indefinite integral, and do not forget to change the limits when you use substitution. A definite integral can be negative even when the geometric area is positive.
study.integral.short_answer: The definite integral is the signed area between a curve and the x-axis. The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus says that integrating a rate recovers the total change.
study.integral.subtitle: Signed area, the Riemann sum and the Fundamental Theorem that links integration to differentiation.
study.integral.theory.0: The area under a graph is approximated by thin rectangles. Split the interval into $n$ pieces and sample one point in each; the Riemann sum is $\sum_{k=1}^{n} f(x_k^*)\Delta x$. As $n\to\infty$ and $\Delta x\to 0$ this sum approaches a number called the definite integral: $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=1}^{n} f(x_k^*)\Delta x$.
study.integral.theory.1: The fundamental theorem has two halves. The first says the accumulation function $A(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt$ has derivative $f(x)$; integration and differentiation are inverse operators. The second makes computation practical: if $F$ is any antiderivative, $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a)$. That is why the table of antiderivatives is the derivative table read backwards.
study.integral.theory.2: Two techniques reverse the two big derivative rules. Substitution reverses the chain rule: with $u=g(x)$, $\int f(g(x))g'(x)\,dx=\int f(u)\,du$. Integration by parts reverses the product rule: $\int u\,dv=uv-\int v\,du$. Choosing $u$ and $dv$ is most of the work; the LIATE rule of thumb suggests algebraic factors for $u$ and exponential or trigonometric factors for $dv$.
study.integral.theory.3: A definite integral is a number, not a family of functions, so no constant $C$ appears. Swapping the limits changes the sign, and regions below the $x$-axis count as negative. That is why it is called signed area rather than geometric area.
study.integral.theory.4: If the interval is unbounded or the function blows up at a point, the integral is improper and defined by a limit. For example $\int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x^p}\,dx$ converges only for $p>1$, while $\int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x}\,dx$ diverges. Both integrands tend to zero; how fast they tend to zero decides convergence, not the mere fact that they do.

study.laplace.key_idea.0: The transform replaces $y'$ by $sY-y(0)$ and $y''$ by $s^2Y-sy(0)-y'(0)$, so initial conditions enter at the start.
study.laplace.key_idea.1: Step functions are handled by the second shifting theorem: multiplication by $e^{-cs}$ delays a function by $c$.
study.laplace.key_idea.2: Partial fractions turn a rational $Y(s)$ into table entries; every linear factor, repeated factor and quadratic factor has its own inverse.
study.laplace.key_idea.3: An impulse is a Dirac delta, and $\mathcal{L}\{\delta(t-c)\}=e^{-cs}$, which is why impulses are easy in the $s$-domain.
study.laplace.key_idea.4: Convolution turns a product $F(s)G(s)$ back into $\int_0^t f(\tau)g(t-\tau)\,d\tau$.
study.laplace.pitfalls: Do not forget the initial terms when transforming $y'$ or $y''$; they are the most common source of a wrong answer. When inverting a term with $e^{-cs}$, shift the whole inverse by $c$ and multiply by the step function. A partial fraction with a repeated factor needs every power, not only the highest one.
study.laplace.short_answer: $\mathcal{L}\{y\}(s)=\int_0^\infty e^{-st}y(t)\,dt$ converts differentiation into multiplication by $s$. Solve the resulting algebraic equation for $Y(s)$, then invert it, using partial fractions or a table, to recover $y(t)$.
study.laplace.subtitle: Turning differential equations into algebra, including discontinuous and impulsive forcing.
study.laplace.theory.0: The Laplace transform is an improper integral that maps a function of time to a function of $s$. It exists when $y$ grows no faster than an exponential, which covers every solution of a constant-coefficient linear equation. The transform is linear, so sums and constant multiples pass straight through.
study.laplace.theory.1: The derivative rule is the reason the method works: $\mathcal{L}\{y'\}=sY-y(0)$ and $\mathcal{L}\{y''\}=s^2Y-sy(0)-y'(0)$. A differential equation becomes an algebraic equation in $Y$, and the initial conditions are folded into the right side instead of being applied at the end.
study.laplace.theory.2: After solving for $Y(s)$ you must invert. Partial fractions split a rational expression into terms matching the table: $\frac{1}{s-a}$ gives $e^{at}$, $\frac{s}{s^2+\omega^2}$ gives $\cos\omega t$, $\frac{\omega}{s^2+\omega^2}$ gives $\sin\omega t$, and repeated factors contribute powers of $t$.
study.laplace.theory.3: Piecewise forcing is written with the unit step $u_c(t)$. The second shifting theorem says $\mathcal{L}\{u_c(t)f(t-c)\}=e^{-cs}F(s)$. In practice you rewrite the forcing in the form $f(t-c)$ first, transform it, and later read the delay from the exponential factor.
study.laplace.theory.4: An impulse at time $c$ is modelled by the Dirac delta $\delta(t-c)$, with $\mathcal{L}\{\delta(t-c)\}=e^{-cs}$. The response to an impulse is the impulse response, and the response to arbitrary forcing is its convolution with that impulse response.
study.laplace.theory.5: The transform is equally useful for systems: each equation becomes an algebraic relation, and a linear system becomes a matrix equation $(sI-A)Y=\mathbf{y}(0)+\mathbf{F}(s)$. Chapter 6 develops this for single equations, and Chapter 7 reuses it for systems.

study.limits.key_idea.0: The limit describes behaviour near $a$, not the value at $a$; a function may have a limit where it is undefined.
study.limits.key_idea.1: Limits respect sums, products, quotients and compositions whenever the individual limits exist and no denominator vanishes.
study.limits.key_idea.2: A two-sided limit exists exactly when both one-sided limits exist and agree.
study.limits.key_idea.3: Indeterminate forms such as $\frac{0}{0}$ need algebra, a conjugate, or L'Hopital's rule, not substitution.
study.limits.key_idea.4: Continuity at $a$ needs three things: $f(a)$ defined, the limit existing, and the two being equal.
study.limits.pitfalls: Substituting $x=a$ into a quotient is not always legal; check that the denominator is nonzero. A table of values can suggest a limit but never proves one. Do not confuse 'undefined at $a$' with 'no limit at $a$': the function $x\sin(1/x)$ is undefined at zero yet has limit zero.
study.limits.short_answer: A limit $L$ means that $f(x)$ can be made as close to $L$ as we like by taking $x$ close enough to $a$, but not equal to $a$. The value $f(a)$ is irrelevant for the limit; continuity is the extra requirement that $f(a)$ equals the limit.
study.limits.subtitle: The definition, the algebra of limits, one-sided limits and the three kinds of discontinuity.
study.limits.theory.0: The informal phrase 'gets arbitrarily close' is made precise with $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$: for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a $\delta>0$ such that $0<|x-a|<\delta$ implies $|f(x)-L|<\varepsilon$. The condition $0<|x-a|$ is what makes the value at $a$ irrelevant.
study.limits.theory.1: The limit laws let you compute almost everything by substitution: the limit of a polynomial at $a$ is its value at $a$, and the same holds for rational functions wherever the denominator is nonzero. When substitution gives $\frac{0}{0}$, factor and cancel, multiply by the conjugate, or use a trigonometric identity.
study.limits.theory.2: One-sided limits describe the two approaches separately. The two-sided limit exists if and only if both one-sided limits exist and are equal. This is how a jump is detected: $f(x)=|x|/x$ has left limit $-1$ and right limit $1$, so no two-sided limit exists at zero.
study.limits.theory.3: Continuity is a local property. A function is continuous at $a$ when $f(a)$ is defined, $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)$ exists, and the two agree. A removable discontinuity has a limit but the wrong value, a jump has two different one-sided limits, and an infinite discontinuity has an asymptote.
study.limits.theory.4: The intermediate value theorem follows from continuity on a closed interval: if $f(a)<c<f(b)$, some $x$ between $a$ and $b$ satisfies $f(x)=c$. This is the existence tool behind root finding, and it is why a continuous function cannot jump over a value.
study.limits.theory.5: The extreme value theorem says a continuous function on a closed bounded interval attains a maximum and a minimum. Together with the intermediate value theorem it gives the geometric facts that optimisation and curve sketching rely on.

study.linear_algebra.example.1.step.2.de: $\det A\ne0$, so the columns are independent and $A$ is invertible.
study.linear_algebra.key_idea.0: The determinant is the signed area or volume scale factor, and a matrix is invertible exactly when $\det A\ne0$.
study.linear_algebra.key_idea.1: Eigenvalues solve the characteristic equation $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$; eigenvectors solve $(A-\lambda I)\mathbf{v}=0$.
study.linear_algebra.key_idea.2: A matrix with a full set of eigenvectors is diagonalisable: $A=PDP^{-1}$ with the eigenvalues on the diagonal of $D$.
study.linear_algebra.key_idea.3: Symmetric matrices have real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors, which is why they are so well behaved.
study.linear_algebra.key_idea.4: The matrix exponential $e^{At}$ is built from the eigenvalues and solves $\mathbf{x}'=A\mathbf{x}$.
study.linear_algebra.pitfalls: Eigenvectors are defined up to a nonzero scalar, so $(2,1)$ and $(-2,-1)$ describe the same direction. Do not divide by a determinant before checking that it is nonzero. For a repeated eigenvalue, verify the dimension of the eigenspace instead of assuming two independent eigenvectors exist.
study.linear_algebra.short_answer: A matrix acts on vectors, a determinant tests invertibility, and an eigenvector is a direction the matrix only stretches. Solving $A\mathbf{v}=\lambda\mathbf{v}$ and $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$ is the whole eigenvalue algorithm.
study.linear_algebra.subtitle: Matrices, determinants, eigenvalues and diagonalisation, the tools behind linear systems.
study.linear_algebra.theory.0: A matrix is a linear map written in coordinates. Multiplication composes maps, the identity does nothing, and the inverse undoes a map when it exists. Most of the theory is about which maps are invertible and how a map looks in a better basis.
study.linear_algebra.theory.1: The determinant is multilinear and alternating in the columns, which fixes it uniquely once we require $\det I=1$. It vanishes exactly when the columns are dependent, so $\det A\ne0$ is equivalent to invertibility. In two dimensions it is the signed area of the parallelogram spanned by the columns; in three it is the signed volume.
study.linear_algebra.theory.2: An eigenvector is a nonzero vector with $A\mathbf{v}=\lambda\mathbf{v}$. Rearranging gives $(A-\lambda I)\mathbf{v}=0$, which has a nonzero solution exactly when the matrix is singular, that is when $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$. This polynomial equation is the characteristic equation, and its degree is the size of the matrix.
study.linear_algebra.theory.3: Diagonalisation collects the eigenvectors into $P$ and the eigenvalues into $D$, so $A=PDP^{-1}$. Powers become easy, $A^k=PD^kP^{-1}$, and the matrix exponential is $e^{At}=Pe^{Dt}P^{-1}$. A matrix is diagonalisable when it has enough independent eigenvectors; repeated eigenvalues may still work if the eigenspace is large enough.
study.linear_algebra.theory.4: Real symmetric matrices are the best case: the spectral theorem gives an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors and real eigenvalues. This is why inertia matrices and covariance matrices behave so predictably, and why the Wronskian and normal-mode analysis are clean.
study.linear_algebra.theory.5: Differential equations use all of this. A linear system $\mathbf{x}'=A\mathbf{x}$ is solved through the eigenpairs of $A$, and a higher-order equation is converted to a first-order system by introducing the derivatives as new unknowns. The eigenvalues then carry the growth rates and frequencies of the original problem.

study.numerical.key_idea.0: The step size $h$ controls everything: smaller $h$ means smaller error but more work and more accumulated round-off.
study.numerical.key_idea.1: Euler is first order, improved Euler is second order, and classical Runge-Kutta is fourth order.
study.numerical.key_idea.2: Local truncation error is the error of one step; global error is what accumulates over the whole interval.
study.numerical.key_idea.3: Stability restricts $h$: for a stiff decay rate the explicit method explodes unless $h$ is small enough.
study.numerical.key_idea.4: Always compare a numerical solution with a known exact solution, a smaller step, or a conserved quantity.
study.numerical.pitfalls: Do not test a method only on a smooth short interval; error often appears after many steps. Keep $h$ fixed and report it, because a result without a step size is meaningless. When comparing with an exact solution, compare at the same grid points, not after interpolation.
study.numerical.short_answer: A numerical method replaces $y'=f(t,y)$ by a step formula. Euler takes the tangent step $y_{n+1}=y_n+hf(t_n,y_n)$; Runge-Kutta samples the slope four times per step and is far more accurate for the same $h$.
study.numerical.subtitle: Euler, improved Euler, Runge-Kutta and the ideas of error and stability.
study.numerical.theory.0: Most differential equations that arise in practice cannot be solved in closed form, so a numerical approximation is the answer. The method produces a table of values $y_n\approx y(t_n)$ on a grid $t_n=t_0+nh$, and the quality of the table depends on the method and on $h$.
study.numerical.theory.1: Euler's method is the tangent line followed for one step: $y_{n+1}=y_n+hf(t_n,y_n)$. It is the simplest Runge-Kutta scheme and the easiest to analyse. Its local error is of order $h^2$ and its global error of order $h$, so halving the step halves the error.
study.numerical.theory.2: The improved Euler method predicts with a full Euler step and then corrects with the average of the two slopes: $\tilde y=y_n+hf(t_n,y_n)$ and $y_{n+1}=y_n+\frac{h}{2}\left(f(t_n,y_n)+f(t_{n+1},\tilde y)\right)$. This is the trapezoidal rule applied to the integral form of the equation, and it is second order.
study.numerical.theory.3: Classical Runge-Kutta evaluates four slopes, $k_1$ at the start, $k_2$ and $k_3$ at the midpoint, $k_4$ at the end, and combines them with weights $\frac{1}{6},\frac{1}{3},\frac{1}{3},\frac{1}{6}$. The result is fourth order, which is why it is the default method in most software.
study.numerical.theory.4: Error has two parts. Truncation error comes from replacing the true solution by a formula. Round-off comes from finite precision. Decreasing $h$ reduces truncation but increases the number of steps, so round-off eventually dominates; there is an optimal $h$, not an arbitrarily small one.
study.numerical.theory.5: Stability is separate from accuracy. For the test equation $y'=\lambda y$ Euler gives $y_{n+1}=(1+\lambda h)y_n$, so the method is stable only when $|1+\lambda h|\le1$. With a fast decay, that forces a very small step even after the solution has become smooth. This is stiffness, and it motivates implicit methods.

study.ode_applications.example.1.problem: A population of 100 grows at 2 percent per year. Find the exponential model and the doubling time.
The growth rate is proportional to the population: $P'=0.02P$ with $P(0)=100$.
study.ode_applications.key_idea.0: State the assumptions and define every variable with its units before writing the equation.
study.ode_applications.key_idea.1: Exponential growth/decay: y′ = ky, so y = y₀e^{kt}.
study.ode_applications.key_idea.2: Newton cooling: T′ = −k(T − Tₘ), so the temperature difference decays exponentially.
study.ode_applications.key_idea.3: Logistic growth: P′ = rP(1 − P/K) gives an S-curve that levels off at K.
study.ode_applications.key_idea.4: Spring–mass and series LRC circuits share m y″ + c y′ + k y = F(t).
study.ode_applications.pitfalls: Keep the units consistent and check that the answer is physically sensible. A negative temperature or a population above the carrying capacity signals an algebra or sign error, not a new phenomenon.
study.ode_applications.short_answer: A differential equation models how a quantity changes. The solution predicts the future state from an initial condition, and the constants in the model come from the physical data.
study.ode_applications.subtitle: Turn a physical statement into an equation, solve it, then read the prediction back in the original units.
study.ode_applications.theory.0: Before any algebra, decide what is conserved: mass, energy, heat or momentum. The rate of change of a quantity equals what comes in minus what goes out. Simplifying assumptions (perfect mixing, drag proportional to speed, constant ambient temperature) must be stated explicitly, because the validity of the answer depends on them.
study.ode_applications.theory.1: The simplest model is exponential growth or decay: $\frac{dy}{dt}=ky$, with solution $y(t)=y_0e^{kt}$. For $k>0$ the quantity grows, for $k<0$ it decays, and the doubling time is $\frac{\ln 2}{k}$. The model holds only while resources are unlimited; real populations bend away as limits appear.
study.ode_applications.theory.2: Newton's law of cooling says the rate of change of temperature is proportional to the difference from the surroundings: $\frac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-T_m)$. The solution $T(t)=T_m+(T_0-T_m)e^{-kt}$ approaches the ambient temperature exponentially, never crossing it. A well-mixed tank has the same structure, with $Q(t)$ the mass of dissolved substance.
study.ode_applications.theory.3: A mechanical oscillator is written with $m\frac{d^2y}{dt^2}$ and damping with $\gamma\frac{dy}{dt}$: $m\frac{d^2y}{dt^2}+\gamma\frac{dy}{dt}+ky=F(t)$. The natural frequency is $\omega_0=\sqrt{k/m}$. When the forcing frequency matches it, the amplitude grows without bound in the undamped model; that is resonance. The series LRC circuit obeys exactly the same equation with $L$, $R$ and $1/C$, so mechanical intuition carries over to electricity.
study.ode_applications.theory.4: Logistic growth adds a carrying capacity: $\frac{dP}{dt}=rP\left(1-\frac{P}{K}\right)$. It is nearly exponential for small populations, slows near $K$, and produces the S-curve. The equilibrium $P=K$ is stable, because for $P>K$ the derivative is negative and pushes the population back.

study.ode_types.key_idea.2: Homogeneous means g(x) = 0; nonhomogeneous equations add a particular solution to the homogeneous one.
study.ode_types.key_idea.3: An initial value problem fixes y and enough derivatives at one point; a boundary value problem fixes values at two points.
study.ode_types.key_idea.4: First-order standard forms include separable, linear, exact, Bernoulli and homogeneous equations.
study.ode_types.pitfalls: Order is not the same as degree. A nonlinear term such as y·y′ or sin(y) immediately makes the equation nonlinear. For a nonhomogeneous equation, never forget the particular solution.
study.ode_types.short_answer: A differential equation relates an unknown function to its derivatives. It is classified by order (highest derivative), by linearity, and by whether the right side is zero.
study.ode_types.subtitle: Mertebe, doğrusallık, homojenlik ve birinci mertebeden standart biçimler, derste kullanılan terimlerle.
study.ode_types.theory.0: A solution of a differential equation is a function, not a number. The function $y=\phi(x)$ solves the equation on an interval $I$ if substitution makes the equation true on all of $I$. The general solution contains as many arbitrary constants as the order, and each particular solution is selected by an initial or boundary condition.
study.ode_types.theory.1: Order is the highest derivative present. An equation is linear when it can be written $a_n(x)y^{(n)}+\cdots+a_1(x)y'+a_0(x)y=g(x)$, so that $y$ and its derivatives appear only to the first power with coefficients depending on $x$ alone. If $g(x)=0$ the equation is homogeneous, otherwise nonhomogeneous. Linear equations obey superposition: a linear combination of solutions is again a solution.
study.ode_types.theory.2: First-order equations come in a small set of families. Separable: $y'=f(x)g(y)$. Linear: $y'+P(x)y=Q(x)$. Exact: $M(x,y)\,dx+N(x,y)\,dy=0$ with $M_y=N_x$. Homogeneous: $y'=f(y/x)$. Bernoulli: $y'+P(x)y=Q(x)y^n$. Each family has its own substitution or integrating factor; identifying the family is half of the solution.
study.ode_types.theory.3: An initial value problem adds the value of the function and enough derivatives at one point. The existence and uniqueness theorem says that if $f$ and $\partial f/\partial y$ are continuous on a rectangle around the initial point, a unique solution exists. The condition is sufficient, not necessary: failing the test does not prove that uniqueness fails. In a boundary value problem the conditions sit at two different points, and there may be no solution, one solution, or infinitely many.
study.ode_types.theory.4: For second and higher order equations, a homogeneous equation with constant coefficients becomes a characteristic equation. Distinct real roots give a combination of exponentials, complex roots bring sine and cosine, and a repeated root adds a factor $x$. For a nonhomogeneous equation the general solution is the homogeneous solution plus one particular solution: $y=y_h+y_p$.
study.ode_types.theory.5: When the coefficients are not constant, other methods take over: power series about an ordinary point, the Frobenius method about a regular singular point, and the Laplace transform for initial value problems with step or impulse input. The shape of the equation and the type of conditions choose the method, not personal taste.
study.ode_types.title: Classifying differential equations
study.second_order.example.0.step.1.deta: $y_h=C_1e^{2x}+C_2e^{-x}$. The two exponentials are independent because the roots differ.
study.second_order.example.0.step.2.deta: The forcing is a polynomial of degree two, so try $y_p=Ax^2+Bx+C$. Substitution gives $A=-2$, $B=2$ and $C=-3$.
study.second_order.example.1.step.1.deta: The forcing $\cos 2x$ already solves the homogeneous equation, so the usual guess fails. Multiply by $x$ and try $y_p=Ax\sin 2x$.
study.second_order.key_idea.0: The characteristic equation $ar^2+br+c=0$ turns the differential equation into algebra; its roots decide the shape of the solution.
study.second_order.key_idea.1: Distinct real roots give $e^{r_1x}$ and $e^{r_2x}$; a double root adds $xe^{rx}$; complex roots give $e^{\alpha x}\cos\beta x$ and $e^{\alpha x}\sin\beta x$.
study.second_order.key_idea.2: The general solution is $y=y_h+y_p$: the homogeneous part plus any one particular solution.
study.second_order.key_idea.3: Undetermined coefficients guesses $y_p$ from the shape of $g(x)$; variation of parameters works for every continuous $g$.
study.second_order.key_idea.4: Two initial conditions, or two boundary conditions, fix $C_1$ and $C_2$.
study.second_order.pitfalls: Do not multiply $y_h$ by $y_p$; the solutions are added. When the forcing duplicates a homogeneous solution, forgetting the extra factor $x$ leaves an equation with no solution for the constants. Also divide by $a$ before reading off $P=b/a$ and $Q=c/a$.
study.second_order.short_answer: A second-order linear equation needs two independent solutions. Solve the homogeneous equation through its characteristic polynomial, add one particular solution of the forcing, then use two initial conditions to fix the two constants.
study.second_order.subtitle: Characteristic roots, undetermined coefficients and variation of parameters for constant-coefficient equations.
study.second_order.theory.0: A second-order linear equation is $a(x)y''+b(x)y'+c(x)y=g(x)$. On an interval where $a\ne0$ and the coefficients are continuous, the solution space of the homogeneous equation is two-dimensional: every solution is $C_1y_1+C_2y_2$ for two independent solutions.
study.second_order.theory.1: With constant coefficients, substitute $y=e^{rx}$ and obtain $ar^2+br+c=0$. Three cases follow. Distinct real roots give two exponentials. A repeated root $r$ gives $e^{rx}$ and $xe^{rx}$, because one solution alone cannot span the space. Complex roots $\alpha\pm i\beta$ give $e^{\alpha x}\cos\beta x$ and $e^{\alpha x}\sin\beta x$, which is Euler's formula applied to the complex exponentials.
study.second_order.theory.2: For a nonhomogeneous equation the general solution is $y_h+y_p$. Undetermined coefficients is the fast route when $g$ is a polynomial, an exponential, a sine, a cosine or a product of these. Guess the same shape with unknown constants, substitute, and match coefficients. If the guess duplicates a homogeneous solution, multiply it by $x$; a second duplication needs $x^2$.
study.second_order.theory.3: Variation of parameters covers every continuous forcing. With a fundamental set $y_1,y_2$ and Wronskian $W=y_1y_2'-y_1'y_2$, a particular solution is $y_p=-y_1\int\frac{y_2g}{aW}\,dx+y_2\int\frac{y_1g}{aW}\,dx$. It is slower than guessing but it never fails.
study.second_order.theory.4: The Wronskian measures independence: two solutions form a fundamental set exactly when $W\ne0$. Abel's identity says $W(x)=W(x_0)\exp\left(-\int_{x_0}^{x}\frac{b}{a}\,ds\right)$, so the Wronskian is either always zero or never zero on the interval.
study.second_order.theory.5: Initial conditions fix the constants at one point and give an initial value problem. Boundary conditions fix values at two different points and may give no solution or infinitely many. That difference is why boundary value problems need their own theory, developed in Chapter 11.

study.series_power.example.0.problem: Find two power series solutions of $y''-xy=0$ about $x_0=0$.
study.series_power.example.0.step.0.titl: Write the series and its derivatives
study.series_power.example.0.step.1.deta: $\sum a_nx^{n+1}=\sum_{n\ge1}a_{n-1}x^n$, so the $n=0$ term of the second series is absent.
study.series_power.example.0.step.2.deta: $2a_2=0$ and $(n+2)(n+1)a_{n+2}=a_{n-1}$ for $n\ge1$. Thus $a_2=0$ and every third coefficient is linked to one three steps earlier.
study.series_power.example.1.step.3.deta: The two powers are independent, so $y=C_1x+C_2x^2$ on $x>0$.
study.series_power.key_idea.0: A power series is substituted term by term; the result is valid inside the radius of convergence of the solution.
study.series_power.key_idea.1: After shifting indices, the coefficient of each power must vanish, which gives a recurrence relation.
study.series_power.key_idea.2: The two lowest coefficients $a_0$ and $a_1$ stay free; every later coefficient is a multiple of one of them.
study.series_power.key_idea.3: At an ordinary point the series always exists. At a regular singular point the Frobenius method starts from $x^r\sum a_nx^n$.
study.series_power.key_idea.4: The Euler equation $x^2y''+axy'+by=0$ is solved exactly by $y=x^r$ through its indicial equation.
study.series_power.pitfalls: Shift every series to the same power before combining; comparing $x^n$ in one series with $x^{n+1}$ in another is the usual mistake. Keep both free coefficients to the end; discarding $a_1$ loses half of the solution space. When using Frobenius, remember that the larger root always yields a solution and the smaller one may not.
study.series_power.short_answer: Assume $y=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_n(x-x_0)^n$, substitute into the equation, shift indices until every power of $x-x_0$ matches, and read the recurrence for $a_n$. Two free coefficients produce the two independent solutions.
study.series_power.subtitle: Series about an ordinary point, the recurrence relation, and the Euler equation near a singular point.
study.series_power.theory.0: Near a point $x_0$ where the coefficients are analytic, the solutions of a linear equation are analytic too, so they can be written as power series in $x-x_0$. This is the content of the existence theorem for series solutions, and it explains why the method is reliable rather than a lucky guess.
study.series_power.theory.1: The algorithm has four steps. Write $y=\sum a_nx^n$ and compute $y'$ and $y''$ by differentiating term by term. Substitute everything into the equation. Shift the summation index in each series until the general term carries the same power $x^n$. Finally set the total coefficient of $x^n$ to zero, which is the recurrence.
study.series_power.theory.2: A second-order equation gives a recurrence that relates $a_{n+2}$ to earlier coefficients. Because two coefficients are never determined, say $a_0$ and $a_1$, the solution splits into $y=a_0y_1+a_1y_2$ with $y_1(0)=1,y_1'(0)=0$ and $y_2(0)=0,y_2'(0)=1$. This is the series version of a fundamental set.
study.series_power.theory.3: When the series is centred at a regular singular point, ordinary power series fail and the Frobenius method is needed. Write $y=x^r\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_nx^n$ with $a_0\ne0$, substitute, and solve the indicial equation for the possible exponents $r$. The two roots may differ by an integer, in which case the second solution may need a logarithm.
study.series_power.theory.4: An Euler equation $x^2y''+axy'+by=0$ is the model case with a regular singular point at zero. Substituting $y=x^r$ gives $r(r-1)+ar+b=0$. Real distinct roots give $x^{r_1}$ and $x^{r_2}$; a double root adds $x^r\ln x$; complex roots give $x^{\alpha}\cos(\beta\ln x)$ and $x^{\alpha}\sin(\beta\ln x)$.
study.series_power.theory.5: Series solutions matter because most equations with variable coefficients have no closed form. The series gives numerical values, asymptotic behaviour and the radius of convergence, which is the distance from $x_0$ to the nearest singular point in the complex plane.
